title: J. O. Mauborgne's 1915 challenge cipher (Manila, 21 Oct 1915, to the Army Signal School, Fort Leavenworth): odd-shift running key from Engineer Field Manual Part V p. 357, plaintext Article 29 of Hague Convention IV; key recovered from the ciphertext alone by a contributor; 89 of 97 words read, read in part

steps.what: Ciphertext taken from Futility Closet's transcription (14 March 2022) of Kruh's 1993 printing, 499 letters in 99 groups of five and a group of four; the original sheet is lost.

Exploratory statistics: adjacent cipher letters have opposite alphabet parity in 333 of 498 pairs (chance 249), which points to tables whose shifts are always odd. Index of coincidence 0.043 (Altifina's page and measured here), R x47 and Z x33 as the most frequent letters.

Test plan drafted by the AI model and approved by the contributor, sealed before any decryption code touched the ciphertext (SHA-256 9e934fd3bb18456766686c67cf99b18d3f3a036311bfec3fec6929179c4c2e92, sealed 15:28:38 UTC by the session's own clock, by the contributor's record). The model's own forecast beforehand was a 2% chance of success.

Search for an English plaintext and an English key text through 338 candidate tables of odd-shift type: the real text ranked first of 41 candidates, about 20 standard deviations above the average of the decoys; planted controls were recovered (contributor's record; the four language-model data files, about 60 MB, are on request and were not re-run here).

The key text was traced afterwards to Engineer Field Manual (Professional Papers of the Corps of Engineers No. 29) Part V, paragraphs 1 and 2, p. 357, with 'Field fortification' at the head of paragraph 2 replaced by 'It' so that the two paragraphs run exactly 499 letters; the plaintext is Article 29 of the Regulations annexed to Hague Convention IV (1907), with a hostile party / who having penetrated / pretenses, endeavors, entrusted, dispatches against the treaty's wording.

The rule reproduces 489 of 499 letters against the plaintext as supplied (491 with the American spellings pretenses and dispatches at positions 69 and 457); ten positions disagree (69, 88, 122, 194, 238, 255, 397, 443, 457, 462), and at four of them (122, 238, 443, 462) no key letter can give the printed cipher letter.

Contributor's checks: re-enciphering gives 489 of 499; with either text shifted one place the counts are 11 and 37, with the ciphertext shuffled 29; a second AI session and his own machine repeated it; the files are hashed and the hash list anchored by OpenTimestamps in Bitcoin block 975480 (not checked here). He published at https://jaketschakka.substack.com/p/the-adventures-of-claude-and-muaddib at 5:01 PM US Mountain time on 11 Nov 2026 (Substack dates the post 12 Nov), by his record: screenshot of the live post; he sent the result to Craig Bauer that afternoon.

Independent check here from the issue's strings and a second decoder (targets/mauborgne1915/decode.py, python3 -I): lengths 499/499/499, hash matches, 489 of 499 reproduced, the ten misses at the stated positions, 495 of 499 positions with an odd shift; plaintext shifted one place 11 of 498, key shifted one place 37 of 498; 2,000 shuffles of the ciphertext give at most 37 exact matches and at most 287 odd-shift positions. Before the strings were sent, the project had found the odd shift at 495 of 499 positions (at most 291 in 2,000 shuffles of its first run) from the public Altifina text and Article 29, with the implied key beginning FORTIFICATION IS THE ART.

Key text checked against the printed manual: the scan of the Third (Revised) Edition, 1909 (archive.org ad-1117984, p. 357, paragraphs 1-2 of Part V) gives, with 'Field fortification' replaced by 'It', exactly the 499 letters of key.txt; the contributor's scan was the fourth (1912) edition (Google Books GLUmAQAAIAAJ, p. 357, screenshot not seen here); a 1917 printing with the same paragraphs is on archive.org (engineerfieldma02deptgoog). The text of Article 29 compared with the Yale Avalon Project copy.

Prior art: no earlier solution found (short web search; Altifina, Chaocipher Clearing House, Kruh and Bauer as summarised by the contributor). Kruh's and Bauer's books were not read here, and the printed letters of Kruh and Bauer were not compared by eye with the Futility Closet and Altifina text by anyone in this record.

Strict count on the words: 97 words, 89 come out of the key uncorrected (91.8%), 8 words each carry one letter read from the sense (endeavors, operations, Thus, penetrated, of, civilians, the, dispatches); the two spelling differences are not holes. Under the 95% bar: read in part. The ten slips are not explained: four are not producible by any key letter (a slip in the cipher letter), the other four may be slips in the printed text, a copyist or the key text.

validation.notes: docs/_validate.py scores a cipher-token-to-reading key; here the key is a running key (book text), every position has its own key letter and no cipher type carries one value. The check run instead is the control in decode.py: the rule applied with the right texts reproduces 489 of 499 letters, against at most 37 in 2,000 shuffles of the ciphertext, 11 and 37 with the plaintext or the key shifted one place, and 495 odd-shift positions against at most 287 in 2,000 shuffles.

outcome.method_basis: The key text and the plaintext were found by the contributor's search over candidate texts using only the ciphertext's odd-shift signal; no plaintext, crib or key for this item was known beforehand (by the contributor's record, test plan sealed before decryption). The key text was then traced to the field manual and the plaintext to Hague IV Art. 29; both are public texts, neither was associated with this cipher before.
outcome.fraction_read_source: reading.md and decryption.txt, words: 89 of 97 words come out of key.txt uncorrected = 91.8%; the 8 words with one wrong letter are holes; the two spelling differences (positions 69, 457) are read as printed. Contributor's count, by letters: 489 of 499 (98.0%), 491 with the two American spellings. Counted here by letters with the American spellings as the cipher gives them: 491 of 499 (98.4%).

credits.note: key text (Engineer Field Manual Part V p. 357, with 'It' for 'Field fortification') and plaintext (Hague IV Art. 29), found with an AI model working at his direction; strings, audit script and screenshots sent in issue #487; may be named publicly

found the 1915 sheet in the New York Public Library and printed it (The Cryptogram, 1991; Cryptologia 17(2), 1993); the ciphertext used follows his printing via Futility Closet, the same 499 letters as on Altifina's research page

gaps.item: eight words with one wrong letter (endeavors, operations, Thus, penetrated, of, civilians, the, dispatches; positions 88, 122, 194, 238, 255, 397, 443, 462)
gaps.detail: whether each slip is in Mauborgne's sheet, in Kruh's printing or another copy, or in the key text of the edition he used cannot be told without the lost sheet or the printed letters of Kruh and Bauer, which were not compared by eye

gaps.item: the printed letters of Kruh (1993) and Bauer (2017, pp. 351-352) against the transcription used
gaps.detail: both are in copyright and were not scanned; the contributor's comparison with Bauer was made by two AI sessions, not by eye

gaps.item: which printing of the Regulations Mauborgne used (a hostile party / who having penetrated / pretenses, endeavors, entrusted, dispatches)
gaps.detail: the words differ from the treaty text in the U.S. treaty series and the Avalon copy; the U.S. Army's printing of 1914-15 was not looked at

texts.label: Mauborgne's challenge cipher, Manila 21 Oct 1915
texts.summary: The first 499 letters of Article 29 of the Regulations annexed to Hague Convention IV (1907) on who is a spy, in the spelling the cipher letters give, stopping mid-sentence at 'for' where the key text ends; the contents say nothing about Mauborgne's own business, the choice of a legal text and a field-manual key are the contributor's finding. Mauborgne meant sealed envelopes with the plaintext and the method to be opened after three months; they are lost.

reading_review.by: integration reader for the project, after the contributor's AI model
reading_review.note: reading.md read against decryption.txt: 89 of 97 words are plain English straight out of the key, eight words carry one wrong letter each and read by sense; no word is in doubt; checked against Hague IV Art. 29 on the Avalon Project copy. No human has compared the transcription with Kruh or Bauer.

outcome.notes: Solution sent by Jacob Houtrouw (issue #487), checked here with an independent decoder. The key is a book text, not a recovered table: the contributor's claim is that the 1915 message is Article 29 enciphered by an odd-shift running key; it reproduces 489 of 499 letters and 495 positions have an odd shift. Order of events by his record only (single issue, own timestamps). Ten slips unexplained; the first sealed envelope (plaintext) and the second (method) are lost, so the rule is not confirmed by Mauborgne.

prior.where: Not found: Kruh 1993 and Bauer 2017 (ch. 8) present it as unsolved, the Chaocipher Clearing House (a 2020 report on Bauer's chapter) says no solution was ever submitted, Altifina's research page (25 Aug 2026, updated 25 Sep 2026) calls it unsolved and does not test a running key; searches of this ledger, the web and GitHub by the contributor (11-12 Nov 2026) and a short web search here (12 Nov 2026) found no earlier solution. Kruh's and Bauer's books were not read here.

human: Jacob Houtrouw directed the work, approved a test plan the AI model drafted, and checked the result on his own machine; the AI model proposed the odd-shift structure and found the key text and the plaintext in a search over candidate texts. Order of events by his record only (see the steps).
